articles.headline: Bijou Date Pushed Back
articles.body:
The tentative distribution date for the 1960 Le Bijou has been moved back from May 20 to May 25, Le Bijou Editor Dennis Appleyard told the Transcript Monday.

He explained that the postponement is due to a delay in scheduling early pictures and meeting fraternity art work deadlines.

Verne Edwards, chairman of the Student Publications Board, said that he feared this failure to meet deadlines would result in further delays by the printers, since they work on a "very tight schedule."

Appleyard, however, was confident that the yearbook would "definitely be back by the 25th."

"Edwards is worried primarily about the distribution problems, especially since the books will come out during finals. We have a circulation staff, however, and it will be their job to distribute the yearbooks to the students," Appleyard said.

He stated that about 100 of the 312 pages in the yearbook have already been printed. All remaining pictures were to be sent in today, he said, and the final copy deadline is Friday.

"We are about two signatures (or 32 pages) behind, but in regard to last year's delivery date, we are in an approximately equal position. Last year the books came on Memorial Day, which will be about the same as our date in relation to finals."

On the positive side, Appleyard emphasized that the color pictures in the 1960 Le Bijou were termed "the best they had received all year" by the engravers, Jahn & Ollier, of Chicago, Ill.

articles.headline: Flemming To Open Republican Day
articles.body:
Arthur S. Flemming, secretary of health, education and welfare and former OWU president, will speak on "The Republican Approach to the Sixties" during Chapel Monday to begin this year's Republican Day at Ohio Wesleyan, Fred G. Burke, director of the Ben Arneson Institute of Practical Politics, announced last week.

Ray Bliss, chairman of the Republican Executive Committee in Ohio, will discuss "The Party in Ohio" during a luncheon in the MUB following the Chapel program.

The afternoon program will include a panel discussion featuring two Ohio Congressmen, Samuel L. Devine, Columbus, and William H. Ayres, Akron; and Arthus Peterson, Republican National Committee Fellow.

Panelists Questioned

The program will conclude with a questioning of the panelists by journalists John R. Beal, Time Magazine diplomatic correspondent, and Michael Reagon, professor of political science at Williams College.

Congressman Ayres, who represents the Ohio fourteenth congressional district, has served on the Veterans' Affairs Committee and the Education and Labor Committee in the House of Representatives. In 1956 he received the AMVET trophy in recognition of outstanding service on behalf of veterans in the Eighty-fourth Congress.

Congressman Devine, who represents the Ohio twelfth congressional district, is a member of the Interstate and Foreign Commerce Committee and formerly served as a special agent to the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Devine also served three terms in the Ohio legislature and was prosecuting attorney of Franklin County until his election to Congress.

articles.headline: SC Group To Check 'Academic Directions'
articles.author: Mike Maharry
articles.body:
A proposal to establish a temporary "Academic Directions Committee" to integrate students in the "on-going" direction of the University was unanimously passed at last week's Student Council meeting, Student Body President George Conrades said.

Junior Frank Ollendorff, who formulated the idea for the committee, was appointed chairman by Council.

In a statement to the Transcript, Ollendorff said, "This committee is a response of Student Government to the concern of the student body over the direction of the University and is mainly for investigating purposes; to find the facts and report to the student body."

The committee, according to Ollendorff, calls for five to ten members, seven of which have already been approved by Student Council. They are Pat Lindsey, tom Grissom, Pat Martin, Dick Adams, Kurt Iverson, Bob Zimmerman and Roger Thaler. Ollendorff expects to get "two or three" more women members by the end of this week.

The committee will interview members of the faculty, Administration, Board of Trustees, church officers connected with schools and graduate school and job interviewers.

The committee will attempt to discover and present to the student body all areas of academic controversy in the University, Ollendorff said, being sure to present the "full story on both sides."

When asked to comment on the validity of the Academic Directions Committee, Student Body President Conrades said, "I feel it is definitely the responsibility of Student Council to voice the opinions of the student body concerning academic policy."

Ollendorff said that "most faculty members have been very receptive and feel this is an area where students should take an interest."

articles.headline: Bob Maxwell Heads Court Next Year
articles.body:
The appointment of junior Bob Maxwell as chief justice of Men's Court was announced in Chapel Monday by Student Body President George Conrades.

Maxwell, a member of Phi Delta Theta fraternity, is a psychology major from Delaware. He has been a member of the men's judicial body for three years, and will be one of two seniors returning to the court next year, along with Bob Richardson.

In appointing Maxwell, Conrades followed the recommendation of Men's Court, made to him before Spring Vacation last month.

Conrades said he had waited to make the formal appointment so he could tie it in with his Chapel speech urging all qualified male students to make application for positions as justices on Men's Court.

Candidates for Men's Court Justices, Conrades said in Chapel, will be interviewed next week. Five positions are to be filled, including openings for two freshmen, one sophomore and two juniors, he said.

Application blanks may be obtained in the Student Government Office through tomorrow, he added, and must be completed and returned to his box in the SGO by noon Friday.

articles.headline: 8 Seniors Win Phi Bete Membership
articles.body:
Eight seniors were elected last week to membership in Phi Beta Kappa by the Ohio Wesleyan chapter, Richard W. Smith, assistant professor of history and president of the OWU Phi Bete chapter told the Transcript.

The newly elected members are Judy Blackburn, Larry Fulmer, Richard Hattwick, Ray Hopkins, Jack Kangas, Ken Morris, Mary Steele and Laurie Taylor.

Qualifications for Phi Beta Kappa membership include a 3.75 grade average for juniors and a 3.5 for seniors.

Candidates must also have had: 1) two years of math in either high school or college, 2) a foreign language in the 200 range or the equivalent, 3) 102 semester hours of liberal studies and 4) 72 semester hours in study outside of their major field.

Professor Smith said that the initiation and banquet will be held on Monday, May 2. The speaker will be Professor Thomas D. Clark, chairman of the history department at the University of Kentucky. Prof. Clark is widely published in the field of Southern History and has been president of the Southern Historical Association and of the Mississippi Valley Historical Association.

articles.headline: YM Prexy To Take Europe Trip
articles.body:
Jim Hering, a junior from Lyndhurst, O., has been selected to participate in the YMCA "Buildings for Brotherhood" project this summer in Turkey.

Hering, who is president of the Ohio Wesleyan YMCA, will spend two months in Europe, working most of the time in a YMCA camp in Turkey.

Through the work camp, the 16 United students and a similar number from Turkey and other European nations will team up to construct part of an actual "Buildings for Brotherhood" project.

Students will build a sea wall, docks and other waterfront facilities. Seminars and informal group life will be an integral part of the work camp, according to Hering.

In what the YMCA calls its "greatest single expansion of the 20th century," the project joins 33 countries in an effort to raise $16 million for 116 urgent YMCA projects all over the globe. North American YMCA's, as their share of the project, have taken a minimum goal of $5 million.

Hering, as chairman of the Ohio district YMCA, will be representing this area as well as his home club. All expenses are being paid by the YMCA and private contributions.

articles.headline: SG Budget Approved
articles.body:
The $2,463 Student Government budget for the second semester was approved by Student Council at last week's meeting, Student Body Treasurer Bruce Buchanan announced.

The new budget is $70 under the figure for first semester this year, Buchanan told the Transcript. It will now be submitted to the Administration for final approval.

The tentative budget calls for expenditures amounting to $1,203 for Student Government committees. An additional $1,260 has been allotted for the Senior Class, YMCA and YWCA.

The budget includes an allocation of $188 to cover the cost of the Delaware City Amusement Tax on the Social Fee, Buchanan noted. He said that this would leave the entire amount collected from the fee, $5,762, available for social programming.

articles.headline: Democratic Day Planned
articles.body:
Although there is "no organization" in the Young Democrats Club at Ohio Wesleyan this year, the Ben Arneson Institute of Practical Politics has scheduled a Democratic Day for May 16, IPP Director Fred G. Burke told the Transcript.

The IPP has not yet obtained a speaker for the Democratic Day, Burke said, for two reasons. "In the first place, because Ohio has already committed itself to Senator John F. Kennedy as the Democratic candidate for President, leading Democrats have been put to work in key states and will not waste time in Ohio," Burke stated.

Non-Committed Are Leary

"Secondly," he continued, "non-committed Democrats are leary of speaking in a state supporting Kennedy."

Prof. Burke declined to say what members of the Democratic Party are presently being contacted to speak at OWU.

The Young Democrats Club, with one known eight-member meeting last month, has defied repeated efforts of Transcript reporters to locate any other semblance of the group's activity.

A check with the Dean of Men's office revealed that no list of officers has been on file since 1957.

No Organization

Dick Smith, un-official president of the Young Democrats Club, told the Transcript, "You have the name, Young Democrats Club, but no organization. There might be a few interested students who'll agree to set up a Chapel program or entertain Democrats when they come to campus. Other than that, there is no Young Democrats Club as such."

Smith attributed this fact to "lack of advisers and lack of support."

A proposed educational program and a faculty debate on "some phase of the Eisenhower administration," which was submitted last month to the Young Republicans Club, never came into effect. Smith admitted that he hadn't checked with the YRC about carrying out these plans.

Commenting on the club's failure to report their officers, Smith continued, "The officers haven't been organized in the past and are not this year."

articles.headline: Tri-Concert Impressive
articles.author: Linda Merkle Transcript Staff
articles.body:
The a capella choirs of Ohio State, Baldwin-Wallace and Ohio Wesleyan gave a beautiful presentation of several religious and secular selections to a half-filled Gray Chapel audience Friday night.

Dressed in tails and black formal gowns, the OSU choir made a striking and somber visual impression. The balance of their voices was outstanding. "Ra Una Canzone" by Vecchi, a short and swiftly moving presenation, was the best-received of their four selections.

The Baldwin-Wallace choir, the smallest of the groups, made up in quality what it lacked in quantity with its presentation of "Liebeslieder Waltzes, Opus 52" by Brahms and "Glory to God" by Rachmaninoff, two of the most beautiful songs of the evening.

The OWU choir's presentation of "Northern Lights" by Palmgren is worth noting for its unusual modern sound. This work ended on such a minor key that it left the audience stunned. "By Babylon's Wave" by Gounod was OWU's best offering.

Ending the concert were two mass numbers which left the audience visibly moved.

articles.headline: Replacements Announced By Board Of Trustees
articles.body:
The Executive Board of the Board of Trustees has named William R. Jones and Ernestine Frazier to fill the vacancies created by the retirement of C. E. Van Sickle, professor of history, and by the resignation of Johnnie Nell Ray, assistant professor of home economics.

David Jennings, chairman-elect of the history department, told the Transcript that Prof. Jones will enter the history department as an assistant professor.

Mrs. Frazier will enter the home economics staff at OWU "probably" as an assistant professor, said Lelia Massey, professor of home economics.

William R. Jones obtained his Ph. D. at Harvard in 1958 and was a Fulbright Scholar in England during 1957-58. Prof. Jones, who is now an assistant professor at the College of Charleston, in Charleston, S.C., is 30 years old. Prof. Jennings said that Prof. Jones will be teaching courses in the areas of ancient and medieval history.

Prof. Jones' field of emphasis is comparable to that of Prof. Van Sickle, who will retire at the end of the academic year after 30 years at Ohio Wesleyan University.

Ernestine Frazier is presently an assistant professor of home economics at Woman's College of the University of North Carolina. The office of the Vice President of the University and Dean of the College said that Prof. Frazier holds a degree of Master of Science in Home Economics.

Prof. Massey said that Mrs. Frazier would be the director of the Home Management House and will teach Home Furnishings.

articles.headline: Students Can Benefit From Inquiry's Results
articles.body:
The formation of a committee to investigate the general and departmental academic situation by Student Council is being met with some surprise and division of opinion by students and campus authorities. To the Transcript, its formation seems a tentative answer to a problem raised in an earlier editorial (Mar. 22) urging Ohio Wesleyan students to rely upon facts rather than rumors in their reactions to University policies.

That there is a desire on the part of the students to know about their University, a desire officially embodied in a Student Government committee, is good. That the committee will be dedicated to finding out about the University's academic policies and its general direction indicates a feeling of responsibility on the part of the students, wished for by members of the student body, faculty and Administration. Informed students will add an element of student-faculty-Administration understanding now sadly lacking on this campus.

BUT THE COMMITTEE MUST REMEMBER, in view of existing controversies and uncertain relationships, that they are bound to mature actions. First of all, they must keep their goals in mind and remember that their job is only to present the facts to the students. This will involve concentration and precise understanding of the faculty and administrative members with whom they come into contact. An ability to discern the true points resulting from any investigation will be essential.

They cannot afford to neglect any problems that arise and they must always equally present all sides of any conflict. It is our hope that the committee will never allow itself to be used as a tool of any one University group at the expense of any other; otherwise it will no longer embody responsibility on the part of the students.

THE MAJORITY OF THE RESPONSIBILITY rests upon the student body, however. There will be no need for ten people to take up the time of the faculty and Administration unless the students are willing to take time to note and weigh the facts and make decisions accordingly.

If the committee and the students continue on the desired plane of maturity, and if members of the faculty and Administration cooperate accordingly, this investigation could prove to be one of the most valuable steps taken by Student Council in a long time. And it should generate optimism among interested persons outside the OWU community as well as among those within, in that the students of this University are showing such an active interest in its affairs.

articles.headline: Forum Book Campaign Merits Student Support
articles.body:
This week's Transcript carries the story of a fund drive for books beginning today under the auspices of Student Forum. A committee, chaired by poet Archibald MacLeish, is conducting the campaign on the national level.

We feel that the purpose of this drive is worthy of our support. In recent years, the Soviets have been making great propaganda gains over the Western nations by distributing the works of great Russian authors among the intellectual and political leaders of the so-called neutral nations.

THE RUSSIANS undoubtedly have realized an advantage which only their own atrocities, such as the 1956 handling of the Hungarian revolt, have been able to counteract. Through no particular merit of its own diplomacy, the United States has not suffered to too great an extent from this distribution of very effective propaganda.

But we have seen, through our own bungling experience with the Hungarian situation, that we cannot always rely too heavily upon our diplomatic resources to balance the effect of Soviet advances in this area. In a situation with which our federal government could not, or at least did not, deal, we must commend those private citizens who, under the leadership of Mr. MacLeish and some of his literary compatriots, have taken steps to fill this dangerous gap in our foreign policy.

THE NATIONAL CAMPAIGN to send books rich in the American heritage of individual liberty and responsibility of these intellectual and political leaders in the uncommitted countries is an example of this liberty and responsibility at work.

At Ohio Wesleyan, members of Student Forum will be soliciting contributions from the members of the student body this week. It is our hope that the students of Ohio Wesleyan University will shed some of their long-lamented apathy and will give generously to this cause. This is our opportunity to show that we are concerned with more than the narrow world of OWU.

articles.headline: Negro Aid
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:
The recent proposal to grant financial aid to Negro students expelled from colleges in the South because of unbecoming conduct connected with racial disturbances is of questionable worth.

I feel that the proposal is bad in that it deviates from the normal criteria used in granting a scholarship. The recent anti-segregation disturbances in the South have been characterized by disorderly conduct and the violation of private property by anti-segregationists.

articles.headline: It Seems To Me...
articles.author: Terry Swango
articles.body:
It seems to me, after reading the extremely interesting and thought provoking article in last week's Transcript by my esteemed friend Mr. Roger Lockwood, that there is more to be said on the provocative topic of physical education grades.

I concur with Mr. Lockwood in his conclusion as to the importance of these grades. I, however, feel that there are several areas of extreme importance much closer to us than Pimlico or Las Vegas. One of these areas which we should consider is that of home economics.

I recently spoke to a coed who has had the importance of phys. ed. grades pointed up to her in the most vital terms. This coed has only been able to obtain C's in the phys. ed. department. This fact has made it obvious to her (in terms of motion study) that she will never adequately be able to iron a shirt. After recovering her rationality, she has been able to resign herself to the fact that she must change her major. If she had never gotten a phys. ed. grade she would never have known until too late that she is unsuitable for homemaking.

Another area where phys. ed. grades could be of extreme value at Ohio Wesleyan is in the selection of the winners of auto permits. It seems logical that any student who has been unable to maintain a B average or better in the field of physical education is insufficiently coordinated to be a safe driving member of the Red and Blue Sticker (Continued on next page)

articles.headline: Open Opinions
articles.author: Jerry Sell
articles.body:
Party Bosses Scoff At Kennedy Victory

Senator John Kennedy certainly must be talking to himself these days! He has known all along that to win the Democratic nomination in the face of opposition from many party "pros" he would have to make an almost unprecedented show of popular strength in presidential primaries.

So he decided to enter every primary in sight. He entered the Wisconsin primary — in spite of the fact that Wisconsin is in Senator Humphrey's own backyard — in spite of its heavy rural population which likes Humphrey's farm policy. When Jack first announced his decision to run there, many predicted it would be his downfall, that he couldn't beat Humphrey there.

Well, last Tuesday he did beat Humphrey there, by 100,000 votes. He got two-thirds of the delegates at stake and if the method of allotting delegates hadn't been rigged against him just before the election he would have gotten even more.

Yet nevertheless, this week many observers have been saying that Kennedy's chances look dimmer, that he didn't win by as much as he should have. They're saying that Humphrey is finished now, but that the chances of the various "dark horses" are much better than they were last week.

Yes, it's very hard to understand, hard for Kennedy to understand, at any rate. He went into a primary in his opponents' own territory. Three months ago the race was said to be neck and neck. He then won by 100,000 votes, getting 56 per cent of the vote, and the experts say he hurt his chances for the nomination. American politics are certainly strange!

Now the experts are saying that Humphrey may beat Kennedy in West Virginia, a state with only three per cent Roman Catholics, a state which is chronically depressed economically and very agreeable to Humphrey's "neo-New Deal" pump priming. Perhaps poor Jack Kennedy will again hurt his chances by winning 56 per cent of the vote.

articles.headline: Good Friday
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:

It would appear that the fine religious nature of Ohio Wesleyan University is somewhat incongruous with its policy concerning Good Friday.

To many, attending services on Good Friday is as meaningful as, if not more so than, attending on Easter. The Administration does see fit to allow a break in afternoon classes at which time we may attend church. However, is the full meaning of the day allowed to permeate the minds of students who must attend these services "between classes" as if treking to the MUB or back to the dorm or fraternity house?

This preparatory day cannot help but lose a great deal of meaning when worship services are worked into a class schedule. Many who would ordinarily attend church at this time will undoubtedly take the easier way out and find the time between 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. on Good Friday good for studying.

Is all this in line with the Christian ethics which the Administration and alumni have recently been so eager to uphold?

(Name withheld by request)

articles.headline: Washington Plan Applications Due

Names of the students chosen for the Washington Semester will be announced shortly after Apr. 23, when applications are due, Professor of Political Science Robert E. Lorish told the Transcript early this week.

Positions on the Association of Women Students' Handbook Revision Committee are now available to OWU women interested in participating in the formulation of AWS policies, said Bonnie Butler, AWS Large Board member.

Miss Butler, Stuyvesant Hall president, also said that those who wish to join any of the eight revisions committees may do so by signing at their respective residence halls.

As a committee member, they may express their criticisms and proposed revisions of any AWS policy. These suggestions will be presented, within the next seven weeks, by Large Board to AWS members for approval or disapproval.

All policy revisions will be effective throughout the 1960-61 school year.

articles.headline: On Campus with Max Shulman
articles.author: Max Shulman (Author of "I Was a Teen-age Dwarf", "The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis", etc.)
articles.body:
"NO PARKING"

As everyone knows, the most serious problem facing American colleges today is the shortage of parking space for students' cars.

Many remedies have been offered to solve this vexing dilemma. For instance, it has been suggested that all students be required to drive small foreign sports cars which can be carried in the purse or pocket. This would, of course, solve the parking problem but it would make double dating impossible—unless, that is, the boys make the girls run along behind the car. But that is no solution either because by the time they get to the prom the girls will be panting so hard that they will wilt their corsages.

Another suggested cure for our parking woes is that all students smoke Marlboro cigarettes. At first glance this seems an excellent solution because we all know Marlboro is the cigarette which proved that flavor did not go out when filters came in—and when we sit around and smoke good Marlboros we are so possessed by sweet contentment that none of us wishes ever to leave, which means no gadding about which means no driving, which means no parking problem.

But the argument in favor of Marlboros overlooks one important fact: when you run out of Marlboros you must go get some more, which means driving, which means parking, which means you're right back where you started.

Probably the most practical suggestion to alleviate the campus parking situation is to tear down every school of dentistry in the country and turn it into a parking lot. This is not to say that dentistry is unimportant. Gracious, no! Dentistry is important and vital and a shining part of our American heritage. But the fact is there is no real need for separate schools of dentistry. Dentistry could easily be moved to the school of mining engineering. Surely anyone who can drill a thousand feet for oil can fill a simple little cavity.

This experiment—combining dentistry with mining engineering—has already been tried at several colleges—and with some very interesting results. Take, for instance, the case of a dental student named Fred C. Sigafoos. One day recently Fred was out practicing with his drilling rig in a vacant lot just off campus. He sank a shaft two hundred feet deep and, to his surprise and delight, he struck a detergent mine. For a while Fred thought his fortune was made but he soon learned that he had drilled into the storage tank of the Eagle Laundry. Walter P. Eagle, president of the laundry, was mad as all get-out and things looked mighty black for Fred. But it all ended well. When Mr. Eagle called Fred into his office to chew him out, it so happened that Mr. Eagle's beautiful daughter, Patient Griselda, was present. For years Patient Griselda had been patiently waiting for the right man. "That's him!" she cried upon spying Fred—and today Fred is a full partner in the Eagle Laundry in charge of pleats and ruffles.

© 1960 Max Shulman

* * *

articles.headline: Dean Urges Early Summer Sign-Up
articles.body:
With 15 applications already received, Registrar Allan C. Ingraham urged students who are behind in hours for graduation and those who are on probation to register for OWU's summer session, which runs from June 8 to July 22.

Dean Ingraham said that most of the applications are expected in late May, but that students should not put off registering to the "absolute last minute," since there is some possibility of too many applications.

Students have until June 10 to register, Dean Ingraham added.

The dean also stated that "the number of students on the OWU campus carrying an excess of 17 hours is currently decreasing. All students who have fallen behind in hours will have to face either overloading or summer school before graduation."

He also stressed that all students with low point averages and those on academic probation should be thinking about attending the summer session.

"The only way that a freshman or sophomore currently in attendance at OWU can raise his point average is by attending OWU summer session.

"The grades earned in the summer session here will be placed on the student's permanent record. Grades earned in any other summer session are not transferred and, therefore, would have absolutely no influence on an accumulative point average," Dean Ingraham said.

He concluded by saying that he felt the summer session would be a definite aid to those students who were planning to accelerate graduation.

articles.headline: Coed Hurt In Mishap
articles.body:
Two people, one an Ohio Wesleyan coed, were injured in a two-car collision early Sunday morning at the corner of Winter and Washington Streets.

Marilyn Groet, a junior from Rochester, N.Y., was admitted for the night to Jane Case hospital suffering multiple bruises. Also injured was John Simpson from Marysville, O., driver of the other car.

Miss Groet was riding in a car driven by Robert Blue, an OWU senior from Chillicothe, O. Blue was driving south on Washington Street when his car was hit by Simpson's vehicle which had just run a stop sign on Winter Street.

Delaware police charged Simpson with failure to yield the right of way. Damage to both cars was extensive, but covered by insurance.

articles.headline: New Committee Set Up By SG
articles.body:
An "Intercollegiate Committee" replacing the former Student Government Five college Conference Committee was established by Student Council at its Mar. 22 meeting.

Student Body President George Conrades announced last week that the committee will correspond with universities and colleges similar to Ohio Wesleyan in size and type of student body in order to learn how these schools deal with problems similar to those encountered by Student Government here.

articles.headline: Faculty To Read Papers At Academy
articles.body:
Seven faculty members and one student, representing three of Ohio Wesleyan's science departments will present papers in their respective sessions at the Apr. 21-23 meeting of the Ohio Academy of Science.

Approximately 24 faculty members and a number of science majors are expected to represent OWU at the 69th annual OAS meeting to be held at Antioch College in Yellow Springs, O.

Associate Professor A. S. Bradshaw and Assistant Professor Joseph K. Hichar will be giving papers in the zoology section.

Assistant Professors R. D. Henry, J. Joseph Klingensmith and J. Gordon Ogden and senior comparative science and botany major Dave Kramer will present papers in plant science. Vice-President and Dean of the University George W. Burns, in cooperation with Professor Richard P. Goldthwait of Ohio State University, will present a paper in the geology section.

The anthropology and sociology section, the only social science representation in the OAS, will hear Associate Professor of Sociology Donald P. Irish give a paper.

articles.headline: Social Fee For Concert
articles.body:
The remainder of the Student Activities Fee budget will be used for another pop concert or dance this spring, according to Student Body President George Conrades.

The proposed social event was discussed at last week's Student Council meeting, and Conrades and Vice-President Alice McAllister were appointed to work out the necessary details.

Conrades said that he and Miss McAllister are already investigating the possibility of getting such "big name" stars for the event as Ralph Marterie or Lionel Hampton. Whether a dance or pop concert is held will depend partially upon student desires and partially upon what stars are available on such short notice, Conrades added.

Student Forum members were asked to sample student opinion and indicate to Council whether a dance or pop concert would be more popular with the students.

The final selection of a band will be handled by Conrades, Miss McAllister and members of the Student Government Social Committee. The event will be held sometime in May, but no definite date has been set at this time, Conrades said.

articles.headline: H. Richard Niebuhr Presents Christian Ethics Prolegomena
articles.author: Jerry Sell
articles.body:
In the four Merrick Lectures he delivered here last week, H. Richard Niebuhr of Yale Divinity School delivered what he considered a "prolegomena to Christian Ethics."

In the initial lecture on Monday evening, he defined the moral or ethical question as "What shall I do?" He said that if one accepts the image of man "the maker" one expects to look to his goals when he is trying to decide what to do.

If one, on the other hand, takes the image of man "the citizen" as valid, one then expects him to look to laws and mores for the answer to his moral question.

"The Responsible Self"

But, Niebuhr maintained, a more useful image is that of man "the responsible self." He is then seen as a creature reacting and responding to those things around him which affect him. This man, in answering the moral question, looks to "what is going on" for his direction.

In his second lecture, Tuesday evening, he pointed out that man the responder is quite different from man "the maker" or "man the citizen." He is caught up in society, his self is caught up with other selves.

Here the concept of "conscience" entered the picture. It is the "approving or disapproving of actions." And, Niebuhr said, the self in its "conscience act" uses other selves as judges. That is, the self approves or disapproves of its actions by using some "other" as part of its criteria—whether that "other" be some imaginary, idealized other self, or many other selves all together inculcating the "ethos" of their whole society.

"The Ultimate Goal"

But, Niebuhr concluded Tuesday evening, just as man "the maker" often looks beyond his own goals to some "ultimate" goal, just as man the citizen sometimes looks beyond his city's law to some natural or "ultimate" law, man "the responder", looking to other selves to answer his moral question, "What shall I do?" often looks beyond them to the "ultimate Other," something "beyond society" in his ethical quest.

The third lecture, on Wednesday afternoon, considered "The Self in Time and History." While the images of "man the maker" and "man the citizen" fail to take sufficiently into account "the self in three tenses" (past, present, and future), the image of man "the responder" realizes that to the self in the "radical now" are ever present the past of the self and the self's hopes and anxieties for the future. And so it is really the self considering all three tenses which tries to answer the ethical question. But history also enters, Niebuhr said. Man responds not only to the past, present, and future of his own self but to the broader sweep. His responses are sometimes determined in the context of bigger history.

And all beings attempt to change their past and future, constantly try to reinterpret their past and their future. So too, he said, we must try to change, i.e. reinterpret, the sweep and meaning of history, that broader context in which we respond. He said that now we often interpret history and the tenses of the individual self according to "the myth of death." It is the myth that we and the cosmos came from nothing and will inevitably come again to nothing.

Must Discard Myth

Niebuhr said that the Christian must discard this myth in favor of a "history of life," a realization that history and the tenses of the self are "surrounded by eternal life," not by eternal death.

The concluding lecture, on Wednesday evening, was titled "The Self in Absolute Dependence." Here his major premise was that this complex and delicate thing, "the self," which so painstakingly developed in the matrix of other selves, in the forge of the "I-Thou" relationship, is always for its being dependent upon a multitude of factors. There is its tenuous connection to the body, its debt to the conscious mind, its reliance upon complex feelings and sensations, etc.

But, Niebuhr said, above all these it is absolutely dependent upon something else, that "inscrutable power by which I am." He noted that man cannot create or destroy his ultimate "selfness." Yet we tend to respond to "all others except the other which gives us being."

The Power is God

At this point, "Niebuhr the Christian" said that "the power by which we are is 'God.'" He said this is a statement of trust that It is a good force. A religious act, he said, is "an act in relationship to the source of life."

Thus, just as all the actions upon me are part of the "ultimate action," all my responses are part of the one "ultimate response — an integrity of self analogous to the oneness acting upon you."

His closing statement, "God, the ground, the source, my home, my cause, my country, my all," is the "prolegomena to reconciliation."

Those of us who heard these Christian lectures on the responsible self may consider well this week our response to the "ultimate act" upon us, the anniversary of which we observe this week.

articles.headline: SC Names Chairmen
articles.body:

Committee chairmen chosen were, sophomore Jim Charlesworth, Academic Relations; sophomore Carol Garrett, Bishop Boosters; Junior John Welch, Student Bookstore; junior John Mitchell, Campus Chest; junior Dave Lehman, Chapel, and sophomore Judy Strimer, Elections.

Also selected were, junior Bob Richardson, Intercollegiate; sophomore Janet Allen and junior Moody Tidwell, Publicity co-chairmen; freshman John Fazekas, Safety; Sophomore Drew Peacock, chairman and sophomore Corky Adams, vice-chairman, Social, and sophomore Anita Garcia, Special Days.

articles.headline: AAUP National Votes On Segregation Issue
articles.body:
The American Association of University Professors passed two important resolutions in the area of segregation at their 46th annual meeting, held last week in Detroit, Mich.

Robert M. Montgomery, professor of religion, and Donald C. Eyssen, associate professor of speech, attended the AAUP meeting as representatives from the Ohio Wesleyan chapter.

Prof. Montgomery is the newly-elected president of this chapter, and Prof. Eyssen is the new vice-president. Their terms are for the 1960-61 academic year.

In one of the resolutions which was passed concerning the problem of integration in institutions of higher learning, the AAUP spoke out against "academic penalties inflicted upon students peacefully protesting racial discrimination."

The group called upon authorities of colleges and universities "not to be misled by public pressures into punitive action which impairs the learning process and destroys the civil liberties of students."

In a second resolution the group again endorsed the principles and actions of the United States Supreme Court "in decisions providing for the elimination of racial segregation in publicly supported educational institutions.

"It again commends institutions, both public and private, which have made progress in implementing the principle that race should not be a condition for educational opportunity."

articles.headline: Forum Backs Book Drive
articles.body:
A campus-wide drive to buy American books on freedom and dignity for politically uncommitted countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America was introduced to Student Forum Thursday, according to Representative-at-Large Lane McGaughy.

The issue was to be introduced by Forum representatives to their respective groups Monday, McGaughy added. Collections will be taken during the week of Apr. 13-20, he said.

The campus book drive is a part of a national drive headed by poet Archibald MacLeish, chairman of the Freedom House Bookshelf Committee.

The Freedom House Bookshelf Committee is collecting money to buy sets of American books on classic statements on freedom and human dignity to combat the flood of Communist propaganda.

According to a letter sent to Professor of English Ruth Davies by MacLeish, "... the world's most widely translated author (is) Lenin, ahead of the Bible."

The cost to purchase and distribute one set of ten books is eight dollars. The set includes writings of John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson, Thomas Paine, James Madison, John Jay, Henry D. Thoreau and Woodrow Wilson.

articles.headline: Classes Move For Services
articles.body:
Friday's afternoon classes have been rearranged because of the hours of the Good Friday service, to be held from 1 to 3 p.m. in Gray Chapel, the University made known last week.

The schedule for classes on Good Friday is now as follows: one o'clock classes will meet at 11 a.m.; two o'clock classes will meet at 3 p.m.; three o'clock classes will meet at 4 p.m., and four o'clock classes will be dismissed.

The annual service is based on the Dubois cantata, "The Seven Last Words," which will be sung by the A Cappella Choir. Following each of the seven parts, a brief comment will be made by members of the faculty and student body.

Those participating in the service will be Howard Maxwell, professor of physics, first word; Willis R. Olson, associate professor of music, second word; Libuse L. Reed, assistant professor of English, third word; Robert B. Fichter, assistant professor of philosophy and religion, fourth word; Richard A. Wengenroth, assistant professor of fine arts, fifth word; Lane McGaughy, president of the Ohio Wesleyan Methodist Student Movement, sixth word, and Richard R. Gay, director of religious activities, the seventh word.

An intermission will follow each of the first six parts.

articles.headline: Time Writer To Speak
articles.body: John R. Beal, diplomatic correspondent in Time Magazine's Washington Bureau, will make three appearances here next week. Beal, a 1926 graduate of OWU, will speak to new initiates of Pi Delta Epsilon, national journalistic honorary, at the Publications Banquet at the Fort Delaware Hotel Tuesday night. He will also address Chapel next Wednesday and participate in Republican Day activities Monday.

articles.headline: Intramural Debates Scheduled
articles.body:
Fraternity entries for Ohio Wesleyan's first intramural debate competition are due today, Edward R. Robinson, associate professor of speech said this week.

The contest is sponsored by Delta Sigma Rho, national debate honorary society, of which Prof. Robinson is the sponsor. Prof. Robinson said that the purpose of the competition is to get students interested in debate.

Dick Hattwick, senior undergraduate fellow, is in charge of the organization of the contest. Hattwick last week sent out invitations to all fraternities and to independent men.

Each competing fraternity will enter two teams, each composed of two men, with one team debating the negative and one the affirmative of the topic, "Resolved that the power of the faculty over the students of Ohio Wesleyan should be diminished."

Starting next Tuesday, the debates will be held every Tuesday night for three weeks. The debates will be held at the fraternity houses of the fraternities that are competing. Varsity debaters, who are ineligible to compete, will judge the contests.

A permanent trophy will be given to the fraternity that wins the competition.

articles.headline: Easton Named Rep To AAUP
articles.body:
Lloyd D. Easton, professor of philosophy, was elected regional representative to the American Association of University Professors at their annual meeting held last week, Professor of Religion Robert M. Montgomery told the Transcript early this week.

This position makes Prof. Easton a member of the ruling body of the association. As a member of the national council, Prof. Easton's term will run from the beginning of the 1960 academic year through 1964, Prof. Montgomery said.

Prof. Easton, who is a past president of the Ohio Wesleyan chapter of the AAUP, came to OWU in 1946 and has been a full professor since 1955.

articles.headline: Bishop Stickmen Host Tough Foes
articles.body:
Within the space of three days this week-end, Ohio Wesleyan's lacrosse team will probably be facing the two toughest teams on its 11 game schedule, according to Coach Fred Myers.

The Bishops will clash with Oberlin, last year's Ohio conference champs, and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute of New York, one of the best teams in the East, in two important contests.

"If we get by Oberlin, there is a good possibility that we will go all the way," predicted Myers prior to the Bishops first home conference encounter this Saturday afternoon at South Field against the Yeomen.

Oberlin Strong
Myers rates Oberlin very high since the Yeomen have been conference champs for the last two years and went undefeated last year. This year the Yeomen have again fielded a strong, well-balanced team led by midfielder Joe Horn and goalie Lazlo Babos who were All-Midwest picks of last year.

The Bishop stickmen will be out for revenge Saturday because of the two trouncings last year at the hands of Oberlin, by scores of 15-5 and 14-2.

RPI Invades
On Monday, the Rensselaer Poly lacrosse squad, rated one of the top teams in the East, will invade South Field to test the Bishops.

Myers believes that RPI will "definitely be good, but we feel we can give them a good game." He also stated that his team will be very strong this year with a lot of experienced players from the previous two years.

New Offence
Myers is planning to hypo his offensive attack this spring by employing three midfield units in the up-coming games. With an extra supply of talent on hand this year, Myers feels he will be able to use any of the three units without hurting the strength of his team.

The "One" unit of Fred Fri, Bob Ginaven and Charles Jantz will be alternated with the "Bandits," comprised of Jack Orin, Dick Hoppe and Max Urick, or the "Seniors," composed of Dick Heaston, Jon Boucher and Louis Schroeder.

On defense, Phil Roos, Dave Hume and Lee Abernathy will start with Chris Hetzel and Jay Farrar ready to step in when needed.

The attack positions will be filled by Rog Auker, "who could be the all-time high scorer for Ohio Wesleyan," says Myers; Jeff Fox, a 6'5" freshman who shows a lot of promise, and Tom "Flash" Howell. They will be pushed by Bill Bishop, Dick Weist and Dave Berger.

Rounding out the starting team will be All-Midwest goalie Thorpe Mitchell.

articles.headline: Sailors Eye Wooster After Opening Defeat
articles.body:
Although high winds at Notre Dame gave the Wesleyan sailors a pain in the sails as they placed fourth in the Notre Dame regatta, Ken Engler voiced optimistic hopes for OWU's chances at the Ohio Champs Regatta at Wooster next weekend.

Ohio State will be forced to send its second team to the Regatta at Wooster, thus giving OWU sailors a chance to win the competition. Oberlin will probably put up the biggest threat to Ohio Wesleyan, but the field remains open between the remaining three schools, Baldwin Wallace, Wooster and Xavier.

Linda Esslinger skippered for OWU at Notre Dame in the A division, and with the aid of Paul Switzer, captured 21 out of a possible 42 points.

In the B division, Joel Saphir, with John Rodrigues as crewmen, snatched 30 out of the possible 42 points.

Saturday was a rough day as far as the weather was concerned, with winds from 25-35 mph. Wayne State was forced to drop out of the meet after several of their boats capsized.

The University of Detroit sailed out on top with a total of 74 points. The favored host sailors from Notre Dame had to be content with a second place. Marquette made a surprise showing in the third place slot with 51 points, while the Bishops were behind with 47 points. The University of Wisconsin and General Motors Institute trailed by a considerable margin to round out the competition.

Ken Engler, club commadore, felt that in addition to adverse weather conditions, the Bishops had to put up with a "poorly run regatta."

articles.headline: Cindermen Open Today Against Winona, Bluffton
articles.body:
Today at 3:30 p.m. the Ohio Wesleyan track team will open its season against Winona State Teachers College of Minnesota and Bluffton College from Ohio.

Nine Bishop lettermen will lead the OWU squad against the opposition. Little is known about Bluffton, but Winona is expected to field a strong team.

The Winona team has made Delaware a stop on its spring tour for the past two years. Each year their performances have improved and it looks like they may outscore the Bishops this year.

The 440 and 100 yard dashes will be featured events. Last year John Guy edged Winona's Marv Roush in 10.0 sec. in the 100 and Winona's Dave Glazier nipped Dave Ross in 52.44 sec. for second in the 440.

Top man for Winona is Dick Anderson, who took second in the NAIA Cross Country Championships last fall. Last year Anderson won the mile and took second to John Gutknecht in the two-mile run.

OWU Coach Sterling Geesman predicts a much closer meet than in the past two years, when the Bishops ran over both teams by large margins.

Weather permitting, and it hasn't permitted such as yet, the track season will get under way in Delaware this afternoon.

Saturday afternoon the Bishops will step way out of their class to tackle Ohio State and Ohio University in Columbus. Eighty-three thousand vacant seats in spacious Buckeye Stadium will enclose the OWU track team as they meet the Big Ten and Mid-American schools.

articles.headline: Strimer Seeks Track Officials
articles.body:
It takes more than runners, jumpers and throwers to make a track meet. Timers, scorekeepers, judges, attendants and inspectors for the different events are needed to keep the meet running smoothly, according to Robert Strimer, director of athletics.

Each year the Athletic Department has asked for and received help from students, faculty and townspeople who will fill these positions.

Strimer said that the High School Relays, held this year on Apr. 30, need the most assistance. Other home meets are today at 3:30, Apr. 27, May 7, May 10 and May 14.

He said that anyone interested should contact the Athletic Department.

articles.headline: Dolphins Place Third In Florida Aqua Show
articles.body:
Seven Ohio Wesleyan Dolphin Club swimmers took third place honors at the international Aquatic Art Festival held last weekend at Florida State University, Tallahassee, Fla.

The OWU swimmers competed against 350 contestants from the United States and Canada, Martha Patterson, assistant professor of physical education, told the Transcript Monday.

The festival was sponsored by the International Academy of Aquatic Arts an organization which promotes synchronized swimming all over Europe and the Americas.

Prof. Patterson listed the OWU entries as follows: Nancy McKain, solo; Thurza Parsons and Anita Zimmerly, a duet, and Frances Alter, Sally Stewart, Larry Lays and Ed Lash swimming in a mixed number.

"Our mixed swimming group was asked to swim at the public exhibition Saturday night," said Prof. Patterson. "This part of the festival was televised for the Tallahassee area."

She also said that the guest of honor at the program was movie star and swimming pool manufacturer Esther Williams, who spoke to the participants and audience.

According to Prof. Patterson, Miss Williams was planning to use television recordings of the performances in a film short she was making in conjunction with Cyprus Gardens. Representatives of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer motion picture company were also present, she said.

Four swimming groups won first place trophies while 10 were awarded second class honors.

articles.headline: Bishops Blast Kenyon 10-7 In Ohio Conference Debut
articles.author: Bob Moyers
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan's baseball team made the most of seven hits Monday afternoon when the Bishops won their home opener over Kenyon, 10-7, in a game limited to seven innings because of darkness.

About 100 chilled but happy fans watched the Bishops grab their first win of the season in near freezing weather. The contest with the Lords was a make-up of a doubleheader that was postponed last Saturday due to snow.

The adverse weather conditions didn't seem to bother the OWU team, however, as the Bishops fought off every challenge presented by the persistent Kenyon nine. Each time the Lords came close, the Bishops rallied behind the sparkling pitching of Dave Johnston.

Allows Five Hits

Johnston, in his five inning stint on the mound, allowed only five hits, but he gave up nine walks that caused him to be constantly in hot water. However, the stocky southpaw proved equal to the occasion, except in the second inning when the Lords scored five runs.

OWU opened the scoring in the bottom of the first with three runs on the strength of shortstop Hal Hendershot's two-run double. After Kenyon exploded for five runs, the Bishops struck back with four unearned runs in the bottom of the second on only one hit. Three Kenyon errors helped the rally along.

After the Lords battled back again to tie the score at 7-7, three walks and a passed ball gave the Bishops the winning run in the bottom of the fourth. OWU added two more tallies in the fifth to ice the game.

Olson Two For Four

Bob Olson rapped out two hits in four trips to lead the Bishops, while shortstop Cal Ellis paced the Lords with three hits, including two doubles.

After two costly errors in the second inning, OWU played airtight baseball defensively for the rest of the game to ease the pressure on Johnston and Toby Aaron, who pitched the last two frames.

Johnston (1-1) picked up the win and Al Frost was charged with the loss.

articles.headline: Press Box
articles.author: Rog Lockwood
articles.body:
According to the calendar and a wild imagination, spring has allegedly sprung. Last week, temperatures soared into the 40's, flowers started to wriggle above the mud, and the local ROTC unit moved outside to defend Edwards Field and the tennis courts. Even the sun appeared, in between snow flurries.

Baseball Coach Les Michael, snowed out of his opener and frozen out of his Saturday twin bill, day-dreamed about spring training games in Florida and Arizona. And Fred Myers' lacrosse squad, pre-conditioned for arctic weather, scrimmaged Kenyon anyway.

But there were signs that spring might really be here, after all. A quick scanning of the pages of the last few issues of this paper reveals that the annual faculty - administration spring cleaning operation is in full swing. Many members of both factions are making preparations to fly from the nest to a better climate.

Unfortunately, no one seems to have noticed the quiet demise of veteran Building and Grounds staff member Lee Fraker, who strangely disappeared in midwinter. There were no letters to the department's chairman, no pictures and no policy statements to the Transcript. All he said was: "That's it, fellers, I guess I gotta leaf."

And contrary to the old adage that "Everyone talks about the weather but no one ever does anything about it, "the OWU faculty has now drafted a resolution to import some stormy Southern weather to Delaware, if sufficient monies can be raised.

These then are some of the signs of the times. But for those who are not convinced, if April is here, can spring be far behind?

articles.headline: Hectic Week In Prospect For Netters
articles.body:
With half a break from the weatherman, Coach Glenn Fraser's netmen will face three strong opponents this week.

Today they meet Muskingum on the Selby Courts, Friday they face Ohio State in Columbus and Saturday they travel to Oxford, O., for a meet with Miami University.

Coach Fraser feels he has the best potential he has seen in years. According to him, the problem lies in having the team ready "both physically and mentally."

"It takes some players three or four matches to find their games." With the weather shortening the season almost every day, the Bishops, except for their Southern trip, have not had the opportunity for sufficient preparation.

Last Saturday, the Bishops were forced to cancel their scheduled match with Ohio State due to the adverse weather conditions.

articles.headline: Linksmen Whip Marietta; Face Denison On Friday
articles.author: Jack Donnan
articles.body:
Bishop linksmen open their home season Friday with the Big Red of Denison, after whipping Marietta College 19-1 last Saturday. Taking medalist honors in OWU's first Ohio Conference match was junior Jud Sayre with a six over par, 76.

Playing between intermittent rain and with a tricky wind, the team averaged 79 strokes against Marietta's high 87. Both teams were obliged to play on the back nine holes of the course as most of the front nine was under water.

The Marietta victory came at a good time for the Bishops. It eased the smarting of an 18 1/2-7 1/2 defeat handed to them at Ohio University Friday. The Bobcats breezed through 18 holes with a 385 stroke total, 18 under Ohio Wesleyan's 403.

Rod Myers, OWU's record holder for match play in varsity golf, was low man for the Bishops with a 77. Ohio U's Bill Santor took first place honors with a 74 for the match.

Home Friday
Friday, the Bishops open their home season against the Big Red of Denison. The linksmen from Granville, last year's Ohio Conference champs, will return with all of last year's team. The Bishops bowed to them twice last year, the second time in the conference championship match.

Host Zips
The following day, OWU will meet Akron here. The Zips had trouble last year, coming in fifth in the conference. According to OWU Coach Dick Gordin, his team should bring home a winning match this time.

The following Saturday, the Bishops will meet Wooster and Wittenberg in a triangular meet at the Delaware Country Club.

articles.headline: Les And Co. Face Two This Week
articles.body:
Oberlin and Otterbein will provide this week's baseball attractions, with the Bishops traveling to Westerville tomorrow to meet the Otters and with Oberlin coming to Edwards Field Saturday.

Last year the Bishops split with Otterbein, losing the first game 9-5 and winning the second 10-1 behind the three-hit pitching of Dave Johnston.

Against the Yeoman this Saturday, the Bishops will be out to reverse a 7-6 loss in the only game between the two Ohio Conference teams last season. Nine errors led the way to defeat in a game the Bishops should have won.

The Red and Black will be out for revenge this Saturday and before the dust clears it should prove to be an exciting day of baseball at Edwards Field.

articles.body:
